gallery.filename: Brookwood Avenue and Howth Road - geograph.org.uk - 458573.jpg
gallery.title: File:Brookwood Avenue and Howth Road - geograph.org.uk - 458573.jpg
gallery.description: Brookwood Avenue & Howth Road A busy junction on the road to Dublin, and the freshly planted sign does have some significance. Unlike the UK, Ireland decided is was pointless buying fuel in litres, and showing road distances in kilometres, but the speed limits were in miles per hour! In 2005 it was decided to bite the bullet, and end this half-way house, gone were the limits of 30, 40, 50, 60 & 70 mph, and all the roads across the country were converted to metric speeds. Just so motorists couldn't say they forgot - these metric reminder signs were erected.
categories: Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland
Republic of Ireland photographs taken on 2007-06-05

gallery.filename: Manor House Convent - geograph.org.uk - 458543.jpg
gallery.title: File:Manor House Convent - geograph.org.uk - 458543.jpg
gallery.description:
Manor House Convent. The original house on this site was built by the Howth family in the later part of the 17th century, and re-fronted in red brick in around 1750. It was known as Bettyville House but later renamed Manor House.
The Dowager Lady Howth lived here from 1835 to 1840. In 1854, it became the home of Richard Kelly, a wealthy merchant who, in 1864 donated the tripartite stained glass window to the new St Assam's Church in Raheny. In 1952, the Manor House was sold to the Sisters of the Poor Servants of the Mother of God, who founded a school. In 1957 the house was demolished, and the present convent building and its school was built, which then became known as Manor House School.

gallery.filename: Raheny Cottages - geograph.org.uk - 458522.jpg
gallery.title: File:Raheny Cottages - geograph.org.uk - 458522.jpg
gallery.description: Raheny Cottages This semi-circular arrangement of picturesque cottages was built just above the old Main Street of, and now lies by the centre of, the village of Raheny. Just behind the camera is the main road, but thankfully it didn't impinge on the cobbled yard. To the right is an old churchyard, built on part of the rath from which the area's name comes, and a few hundred metres away is the Santry River, which flows into Dublin Bay opposite North Bull Island.
